```{r setup, include = FALSE}
has_survival <- requireNamespace("survival", quietly = TRUE)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 96,
                      eval = has_survival)
```

A parametric model describes the whole distribution of the time to the event: smooth survival
and hazard curves, quantiles such as the median, time ratios, and extrapolation beyond follow-up.
A cure model adds a fraction of subjects who will never have the event. This vignette shows how
to choose a distribution, read the coefficients, check the fit and use the model.

```{r}
library(SurvX)
lung <- survival::lung
lung$status <- lung$status - 1
lung$sex <- factor(lung$sex, 1:2, c("male", "female"))
lung$years <- lung$time / 365.25
```

## 1. What shape has the hazard?

The non-parametric hazard shows the shape any distribution must reproduce:

```{r hz, fig.height = 4}
plot(hazard_np(Event(years, status) ~ 1, lung))
```

`dist_plot()` gives the linearising plots of the classic distributions; the panel with the
straightest lines points to a candidate:

```{r dist, fig.height = 6}
dist_plot(Event(years, status) ~ sex, lung)
```

## 2. Fitting and comparing distributions

```{r}
fw <- parsurv(Event(years, status) ~ sex + age, lung, baseline = "weibull")
fl <- parsurv(Event(years, status) ~ sex + age, lung, baseline = "lognormal")
fgg <- parsurv(Event(years, status) ~ sex + age, lung, baseline = "gengamma")
fr <- parsurv(Event(years, status) ~ sex + age, lung, baseline = "rp", df = 3)
AIC(fw, fl, fgg, fr)
```

The generalized gamma contains the Weibull ($Q = 1$) and the log-normal ($Q = 0$): its estimate of
$Q$ says which of the two the data favour.

```{r}
summary(fgg)
```

The fitted hazard against the non-parametric one is the visual check:

```{r hzplot, fig.height = 4}
hazard_plot(list(Weibull = fw, "log-normal" = fl, spline = fr))
```

## 3. Hazard ratios and time ratios

The Weibull model can be written in both forms. As a proportional hazards model it gives hazard
ratios, as in a Cox model:

```{r}
fw
```

As an accelerated failure time model it gives **time ratios**: by how much the time to death is
stretched or shrunk.

```{r}
fa <- parsurv(Event(years, status) ~ sex + age, lung, baseline = "weibull", scale = "AFT")
fa
```

A time ratio above 1 means longer survival: women's survival times are about
`r round(exp(coef(fa)[["sexfemale"]]), 2)` times those of men of the same age. The hazard ratio
and the time ratio of the Weibull model are linked by $\beta_{PH} = -\beta_{AFT}/\sigma$, so they
always point in opposite directions for the same effect.

## 4. Predictions and extrapolation

```{r}
nd <- data.frame(sex = c("male", "female"), age = 65)
predict(fw, nd, times = c(1, 2, 5), se = TRUE)$est        # survival
predict(fw, nd, type = "quantile", p = 0.5)              # median survival time
predict(fw, nd, times = 3, type = "rmst")                # restricted mean over 3 years
```

Beyond the last follow-up time, the curve is determined by the distribution alone. Distributions
that fit the data equally well can extrapolate very differently, so compare them before relying on
one:

```{r extrap}
tt <- seq(0.05, 5, by = 0.05)
s_w <- predict(fw, nd[2, ], times = tt)[1, ]
s_l <- predict(fl, nd[2, ], times = tt)[1, ]
plot(tt, s_w, type = "l", lwd = 2, ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "years", ylab = "survival",
     main = "woman aged 65")
lines(tt, s_l, lwd = 2, lty = 2)
abline(v = max(lung$years), col = "grey")
legend("topright", c("Weibull", "log-normal", "end of follow-up"), lty = c(1, 2, 1),
       col = c("black", "black", "grey"), bty = "n")
```

## 5. Cure models

When follow-up is long and the Kaplan-Meier curve levels off, part of the population may never
have the event. The `colon` data of **survival** (adjuvant chemotherapy for colon cancer) show this
for recurrence:

```{r}
colon <- survival::colon
rec <- colon[colon$etype == 1, ]
rec$years <- rec$time / 365.25
```

```{r km-colon, fig.height = 5}
plot(km(Event(years, status) ~ rx, rec), risk.table = FALSE)
```

The curves flatten after about four years. A mixture cure model separates the two questions:
*who is cured?* (the cured fraction, a logistic model) and *when do the others recur?* (the
latency, here a Weibull model):

```{r}
cf <- cure(Event(years, status) ~ rx, rec, cure = ~ rx + node4)
cf
```

The cure coefficients are odds ratios of being cured; the latency coefficients are hazard ratios
among patients who will recur. The predicted cured fraction for each treatment, with and without
more than four positive nodes:

```{r}
ndc <- expand.grid(rx = levels(rec$rx), node4 = 0:1)
cbind(ndc, round(predict(cf, ndc, type = "cured", se = TRUE)$est, 3))
```

```{r cure-plot}
plot(cf)
```

The fitted population survival should follow the Kaplan-Meier curve, and its plateau is the
average cured fraction. When there is no plateau in the data, the cured fraction is not identified
and the fit is flagged.

## 6. Interval-censored data and shared frailty

Every distribution of `parsurv()` can also be fitted to events found at visits, with
`Interval(left, right)` on the left-hand side; `plot()` then compares the fit with the Turnbull
estimate of `turnbull()`. For clustered data, `+ frailty(id)` adds a shared gamma frailty to any
distribution:

```r
parsurv(Interval(left, right) ~ trt + age, data, baseline = "weibull")
parsurv(Event(time, status) ~ trt + age + frailty(centre), data, baseline = "gompertz")
```

Both are illustrated in the survival analysis vignette (sections 10 and 11).

  functions for the generalized gamma distribution. *Statistics in Medicine*, 26, 4352-4374.
* Farewell VT (1982). The use of mixture models for the analysis of survival data with long-term
  survivors. *Biometrics*, 38, 1041-1046.
* Amico M, Van Keilegom I (2018). Cure models in survival analysis. *Annual Review of Statistics
  and Its Application*, 5, 311-342.
* Moertel CG, et al. (1990). Levamisole and fluorouracil for adjuvant therapy of resected colon
